question_text: A 26-year-old nurse presents 12 hours after she accidentally stuck herself with a blood-contaminated needle. She reported the accident appropriately and now seeks post-exposure prophylaxis. She does not have any complaints at the moment of presentation. Her vital signs include: blood pressure 125/80 mm Hg, heart rate 71/min, respiratory rate 15/min, and temperature 36.5℃ (97.7℉). Physical examination is unremarkable. The nurse has prescribed a post-exposure prophylaxis regimen which includes tenofovir, emtricitabine, and raltegravir. How will tenofovir change the maximum reaction rate (Vm) and Michaelis constant (Km) of the viral reverse transcriptase?

                    ### Question
                    A 26-year-old nurse presents 12 hours after she accidentally stuck herself with a blood-contaminated needle. She reported the accident appropriately and now seeks post-exposure prophylaxis. She does not have any complaints at the moment of presentation. Her vital signs include: blood pressure 125/80 mm Hg, heart rate 71/min, respiratory rate 15/min, and temperature 36.5℃ (97.7℉). Physical examination is unremarkable. The nurse has prescribed a post-exposure prophylaxis regimen which includes tenofovir, emtricitabine, and raltegravir. How will tenofovir change the maximum reaction rate (Vm) and Michaelis constant (Km) of the viral reverse transcriptase?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Vm will decrease, Km will stay the same
opb. Vm and Km will both decrease
opc. Vm will decrease, Km will increase
opd. Vm will stay the same, Km will increase
ope. Vm and Km will both increase

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
Tenofovir is a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) that acts by competing with natural nucleotides for incorporation into the viral DNA by reverse transcriptase. As a competitive inhibitor, tenofovir increases the Michaelis constant (Km) because it competes with the natural substrate for the active site, but it does not change the maximum reaction rate (Vm) of the enzyme. This is consistent with the standard biochemical understanding of competitive inhibition, where Km increases due to the need for a higher substrate concentration to achieve half-maximal enzyme activity, while Vm remains unchanged because the inhibitor does not affect the enzyme's catalytic potential at saturation. Therefore, the correct interpretation is that tenofovir will increase Km and Vm will stay the same, aligning with option 'opd'.
